concepts.name: Vector
concepts.statement: A vector is a quantity that has both magnitude and direction; in a plane it is represented by a directed line segment, an arrow, and it is denoted by a boldface letter such as v.

concepts.name: Initial point
concepts.statement: The initial point of a vector is the starting point of the directed line segment that represents it.

concepts.name: Terminal point
concepts.statement: The terminal point of a vector is the endpoint of the directed line segment that represents it; an arrow from the initial point to the terminal point indicates the vector’s direction.

concepts.name: Magnitude of a vector
concepts.statement: The magnitude ‖v‖ of a vector is the length of the line segment that represents it; for v = ⟨x, y⟩ it is ‖v‖ = √(x² + y²), so ‖v‖ ≥ 0, and ‖v‖ = 0 if and only if v = 0.

concepts.name: Zero vector
concepts.statement: The zero vector 0 is the vector whose initial point and terminal point are the same; it is the only vector without a direction, and by convention it can be considered to have any direction convenient to the problem.

concepts.name: Equivalent vectors
concepts.statement: Vectors are equivalent if they have the same magnitude and direction; equivalent vectors are treated as equal, v = w, even if they have different initial points.

concepts.name: Parallel vectors
concepts.statement: Two vectors are parallel if they have the same or opposite directions; two nonzero vectors u and v are parallel if and only if u = kv for some scalar k, and the zero vector is considered parallel to all vectors.

concepts.name: Scalar
concepts.statement: A scalar is a real number; unlike a vector, a scalar has a magnitude only, but no direction.

concepts.name: Scalar multiplication
concepts.statement: The product kv of a vector v and a scalar k is a vector with magnitude |k| times the magnitude of v, with the direction of v if k > 0 and the opposite direction if k < 0; if k = 0 or v = 0, then kv = 0, and (−1)v is written −v. In components, k⟨x₁, y₁⟩ = ⟨kx₁, ky₁⟩.

concepts.name: Vector addition
concepts.statement: The sum v + w is constructed by placing the initial point of w at the terminal point of v; the vector sum is the vector from the initial point of v to the terminal point of w. In components, ⟨x₁, y₁⟩ + ⟨x₂, y₂⟩ = ⟨x₁ + x₂, y₁ + y₂⟩.

concepts.name: Triangle method
concepts.statement: To add two vectors by the triangle method, place the initial point of the second at the terminal point of the first; the sum is the third side of the triangle, from the initial point of the first to the terminal point of the second.

concepts.name: Parallelogram method
concepts.statement: To add two vectors by the parallelogram method, place them with the same initial point and draw the parallelogram with the vectors as two adjacent sides; the sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram from the shared initial point.

concepts.name: Vector difference
concepts.statement: The vector difference v − w is v + (−w) = v + (−1)w; it is drawn from the terminal point of w to the terminal point of v when v and w share an initial point.

concepts.name: Triangle inequality for vectors
concepts.statement: Because v, w and v + w form the sides of a triangle, ‖v + w‖ ≤ ‖v‖ + ‖w‖, with equality only when v and w have the same direction.

concepts.name: Standard-position vector
concepts.statement: A vector with its initial point at the origin is a standard-position vector; it is described by the coordinates of its terminal point.

concepts.name: Component form of a vector
concepts.statement: The vector with initial point (0, 0) and terminal point (x, y) can be written in component form as v = ⟨x, y⟩, with angle brackets for a vector and parentheses for a point; the scalars x and y are the components of v.

concepts.name: Component form of a vector from its points
concepts.statement: If v has initial point (xᵢ, yᵢ) and terminal point (xₜ, yₜ), then v = ⟨xₜ − xᵢ, yₜ − yᵢ⟩: subtract the coordinates of the initial point from those of the terminal point.

concepts.name: Properties of vector operations
concepts.statement: For vectors u, v, w and scalars r, s: u + v = v + u; (u + v) + w = u + (v + w); u + 0 = u; u + (−u) = 0; r(su) = (rs)u; (r + s)u = ru + su; r(u + v) = ru + rv; 1u = u and 0u = 0.

concepts.name: Components from magnitude and direction
concepts.statement: If a vector v forms the angle θ with the positive x-axis, its components are ⟨‖v‖cos θ, ‖v‖sin θ⟩, the legs of a right triangle with the vector as its hypotenuse.

concepts.name: Unit vector
terms: unit vector in the direction of
concepts.statement: A unit vector is a vector with magnitude 1; for any nonzero vector v, u = (1/‖v‖)v is the unit vector in the direction of v.

concepts.name: Normalization
concepts.statement: Normalization is using scalar multiplication to find a unit vector with a given direction: multiply the vector by the reciprocal of its magnitude.

concepts.name: Standard unit vectors
concepts.statement: The standard unit vectors are i = ⟨1, 0⟩ and j = ⟨0, 1⟩, unit vectors along the coordinate axes; any vector can be written as the linear combination v = ⟨x, y⟩ = xi + yj.

concepts.name: Three-dimensional rectangular coordinate system
concepts.statement: The three-dimensional rectangular coordinate system consists of three perpendicular axes, the x-, y- and z-axes, meeting at the origin; every point in space is described by an ordered triple (x, y, z), and the system is denoted ℝ³.

concepts.name: Right-hand rule
concepts.statement: The coordinate axes follow the right-hand rule: when the fingers of the right hand point along the positive x-axis and curl toward the positive y-axis, the thumb points along the positive z-axis.

concepts.name: Coordinate planes
concepts.statement: Each pair of coordinate axes forms a coordinate plane: the xy-plane {(x, y, 0)}, the xz-plane {(x, 0, z)} and the yz-plane {(0, y, z)}.

concepts.name: Octants
concepts.statement: The coordinate planes divide space into eight regions about the origin, called octants; points in an octant have three nonzero coordinates.

concepts.name: Distance between two points in space
concepts.statement: The distance d between points (x₁, y₁, z₁) and (x₂, y₂, z₂) is d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²), the length of the diagonal of the rectangular prism with the two points as opposite corners.

concepts.name: Equations of planes parallel to coordinate planes
concepts.statement: The plane parallel to the xy-plane through (a, b, c) is z = c, the plane parallel to the xz-plane is y = b, and the plane parallel to the yz-plane is x = a.

concepts.name: Sphere
concepts.statement: A sphere is the set of all points in space equidistant from a fixed point, the center of the sphere; the distance from the center to a point on the sphere is the radius.

concepts.name: Standard equation of a sphere
concepts.statement: The sphere with center (a, b, c) and radius r can be represented by the equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² + (z − c)² = r², the standard equation of a sphere.

concepts.name: Vectors in three dimensions
concepts.statement: A three-dimensional vector v = ⟨x, y, z⟩ is the directed line segment from (0, 0, 0) to (x, y, z); with the standard unit vectors i = ⟨1, 0, 0⟩, j = ⟨0, 1, 0⟩ and k = ⟨0, 0, 1⟩, v = xi + yj + zk, and 0 = ⟨0, 0, 0⟩.

concepts.name: Properties of vectors in space
concepts.statement: For v = ⟨x₁, y₁, z₁⟩, w = ⟨x₂, y₂, z₂⟩ and a scalar k: kv = ⟨kx₁, ky₁, kz₁⟩; v + w = ⟨x₁ + x₂, y₁ + y₂, z₁ + z₂⟩; v − w = ⟨x₁ − x₂, y₁ − y₂, z₁ − z₂⟩; ‖v‖ = √(x₁² + y₁² + z₁²); and v/‖v‖ is the unit vector in the direction of v ≠ 0.

concepts.name: Graphing equations in three dimensions
concepts.statement: The same equation can describe a point, a line or a plane in ℝ, ℝ² and ℝ³; to graph an equation in space, find which coordinates it restricts (a product equal to zero gives the union of the sets where each factor is zero, and an equation free of one variable extends its graph in that variable’s direction).

concepts.name: Dot product
concepts.statement: The dot product of u = ⟨u₁, u₂, u₃⟩ and v = ⟨v₁, v₂, v₃⟩ is the scalar u·v = u₁v₁ + u₂v₂ + u₃v₃, the sum of the products of the components; it is also called the scalar product or inner product.

concepts.name: Properties of the dot product
concepts.statement: For vectors u, v, w and a scalar c: u·v = v·u; u·(v + w) = u·v + u·w; c(u·v) = (cu)·v = u·(cv); and v·v = ‖v‖².

concepts.name: Angle between two vectors
concepts.statement: Two nonzero vectors placed in standard position form an angle θ between them, the smallest one, with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π.

concepts.name: Dot product and the angle between vectors
concepts.statement: The dot product of two vectors is the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them, u·v = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ, so cos θ = u·v/(‖u‖‖v‖) gives the angle between nonzero vectors.

concepts.name: Orthogonal vectors
concepts.statement: The nonzero vectors u and v are orthogonal, forming a right angle when placed in standard position, if and only if u·v = 0; vectors are orthogonal, lines perpendicular, and normal is used of a plane or surface.

concepts.name: Direction angles
concepts.statement: The angles a nonzero vector forms with the coordinate axes, α with i, β with j and γ with k, are its direction angles.

concepts.name: Direction cosines
concepts.statement: The cosines of a vector’s direction angles are its direction cosines; for v, cos α = v·i/‖v‖, and likewise with j and k.

concepts.name: Vector projection
concepts.statement: The vector projection of v onto u is the component of v that acts in the direction of u, proj_u v = (u·v/‖u‖²)u; it has the initial point of u and v, the direction of u, and the opposite direction when the angle between them is obtuse.

concepts.name: Scalar projection
concepts.statement: The scalar projection of v onto u, the length of the vector projection, is comp_u v = u·v/‖u‖.

concepts.name: Resolving a vector into orthogonal components
terms: resolution of a vector into components
concepts.statement: To decompose v into orthogonal components with one in the direction of u, take p = proj_u v and q = v − p; then v = p + q and p·q = 0.

concepts.name: Work done by a constant force
concepts.statement: When a constant force F moves an object in a straight line from P to Q, acting at an angle θ from the line of motion, the work done is W = F·PQ⃗ = ‖F‖‖PQ⃗‖cos θ, the dot product of the force and the displacement.

concepts.name: Cross product
concepts.statement: The cross product of u = ⟨u₁, u₂, u₃⟩ and v = ⟨v₁, v₂, v₃⟩ is the vector u × v = (u₂v₃ − u₃v₂)i − (u₁v₃ − u₃v₁)j + (u₁v₂ − u₂v₁)k, orthogonal to both u and v; it is also called the vector product.

concepts.name: Direction of the cross product
concepts.statement: The direction of u × v is given by the right-hand rule: with the fingers of the right hand along u, curled toward v, the thumb points along u × v; so v × u points the opposite way.

concepts.name: Cross products of the standard unit vectors
concepts.statement: i × i = j × j = k × k = 0; i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j; and j × i = −k, k × j = −i, i × k = −j.

concepts.name: Properties of the cross product
concepts.statement: For vectors u, v, w and a scalar c: u × v = −(v × u) (anticommutative); u × (v + w) = u × v + u × w; c(u × v) = (cu) × v = u × (cv); u × 0 = 0 × u = 0; v × v = 0; and u·(v × w) = (u × v)·w.

concepts.name: Magnitude of the cross product
concepts.statement: If θ is the angle between u and v, then ‖u × v‖ = ‖u‖‖v‖sin θ.

concepts.name: Determinant
terms: expansion of the determinant along the first row
concepts.statement: A determinant is a real number associated with a square matrix: a 2 × 2 determinant is a₁b₂ − b₁a₂, and a 3 × 3 determinant is defined by expansion along the first row, each entry of the first row times the 2 × 2 determinant left when its row and column are crossed out, with the middle term subtracted.

concepts.name: Cross product calculated by a determinant
concepts.statement: The cross product u × v is the determinant with i, j, k in the first row, the components of u in the second and those of v in the third, expanded along the first row.

concepts.name: Area of a parallelogram
concepts.statement: If vectors u and v form adjacent sides of a parallelogram, its area is ‖u × v‖, its base ‖u‖ times its height ‖v‖sin θ; a triangle with those sides has half that area.

concepts.name: Triple scalar product
concepts.statement: The triple scalar product of u, v and w is u·(v × w), the dot product of a vector with the cross product of two others; it is the determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix whose rows are the components of u, v and w, and it changes sign when two of the vectors trade places.

concepts.name: Parallelepiped
concepts.statement: A parallelepiped is a three-dimensional prism with six faces that are each parallelograms; three vectors with one initial point, not in one plane, form three of its edges.

concepts.name: Volume of a parallelepiped
concepts.statement: The volume of a parallelepiped with adjacent edges u, v and w is the absolute value of the triple scalar product, V = |u·(v × w)|, the area ‖v × w‖ of its base times its height ‖proj_{v×w} u‖; the triple scalar product is zero exactly when the vectors are coplanar.

concepts.name: Torque
concepts.statement: Torque τ measures the tendency of a force to produce rotation about an axis: if r runs from a point on the axis of rotation to the point where the force F is applied, τ = r × F, and ‖τ‖ = ‖r‖‖F‖sin θ.

concepts.name: Direction vector
concepts.statement: A direction vector of a line in space is a vector parallel to the line, used to describe its direction.

concepts.name: Vector equation of a line
concepts.statement: A line through P(x₀, y₀, z₀) with direction vector v = ⟨a, b, c⟩ is described by r = r₀ + tv, where r = ⟨x, y, z⟩ and r₀ = ⟨x₀, y₀, z₀⟩ is the position vector of P, since PQ⃗ = tv for every point Q on the line.

concepts.name: Parametric equations of a line
concepts.statement: A line L parallel to v = ⟨a, b, c⟩ through P(x₀, y₀, z₀) is described by the parametric equations x = x₀ + ta, y = y₀ + tb, z = z₀ + tc; they are not unique.

concepts.name: Symmetric equations of a line
concepts.statement: If a, b and c are all nonzero, the line parallel to ⟨a, b, c⟩ through (x₀, y₀, z₀) is described by the symmetric equations (x − x₀)/a = (y − y₀)/b = (z − z₀)/c.

concepts.name: Equation of a line segment
concepts.statement: The line segment from P to Q, with position vectors p and q, is r = (1 − t)p + tq for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1; in components x = x₀ + t(x₁ − x₀), y = y₀ + t(y₁ − y₀), z = z₀ + t(z₁ − z₀), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

concepts.name: Distance from a point to a line
concepts.statement: If a line L passes through P with direction vector v and M is a point not on L, the distance from M to L, the length of the perpendicular segment, is d = ‖PM⃗ × v‖/‖v‖, the height of the parallelogram on PM⃗ and v.

concepts.name: Skew lines
concepts.statement: Two lines in space that are not parallel and do not intersect are skew lines.

concepts.name: Classifying lines in space
concepts.statement: Two lines in space are equal, parallel but not equal, intersecting or skew, decided by whether their direction vectors are parallel and whether they share a point (solving their parametric equations together).

concepts.name: Normal vector
concepts.statement: A normal vector n of a plane is a vector perpendicular to it: every vector PQ⃗ between points of the plane is orthogonal to n.

concepts.name: Vector equation of a plane
concepts.statement: Given a point P and a vector n, the set of all points Q satisfying n·PQ⃗ = 0 forms a plane; n·PQ⃗ = 0 is the vector equation of the plane.

concepts.name: Scalar equation of a plane
terms: general form of the equation of a plane
concepts.statement: The scalar equation of the plane through P = (x₀, y₀, z₀) with normal vector n = ⟨a, b, c⟩ is a(x − x₀) + b(y − y₀) + c(z − z₀) = 0, which can be written in the general form ax + by + cz + d = 0 with d = −ax₀ − by₀ − cz₀.

concepts.name: Distance from a point to a plane
concepts.statement: If a plane with normal vector n passes through Q, the distance from the plane to a point P not in it is d = ‖proj_n QP⃗‖ = |comp_n QP⃗| = |QP⃗·n|/‖n‖; for the plane ax + by + cz + k = 0 and P(x₀, y₀, z₀), d = |ax₀ + by₀ + cz₀ + k|/√(a² + b² + c²).

concepts.name: Parallel and intersecting planes
concepts.statement: Two distinct planes are parallel, when their normal vectors are parallel, or they intersect, and the intersection of two nonparallel planes is always a line; the distance between parallel planes is the distance from a point of one to the other.

concepts.name: Angle between two planes
concepts.statement: The angle θ between two intersecting planes has the measure of the angle between their normal vectors, cos θ = |n₁·n₂|/(‖n₁‖‖n₂‖).

concepts.name: Surface
concepts.statement: Planes, spheres and cylinders are examples of three-dimensional figures called surfaces, which can be graphed in a three-dimensional coordinate system.

concepts.name: Cylindrical surface
concepts.statement: A set of lines parallel to a given line passing through a given curve is a cylindrical surface, or cylinder; any curve in one of the coordinate planes extends to a cylinder, such as x² + y² = 9 in space.

concepts.name: Rulings
concepts.statement: The parallel lines that make up a cylinder are its rulings.

concepts.name: Trace
concepts.statement: The traces of a surface are the cross-sections created when it intersects a plane parallel to one of the coordinate planes; to find the trace in the xy-, yz- or xz-plane, set z = 0, x = 0 or y = 0.

concepts.name: Quadric surface
concepts.statement: Quadric surfaces are the graphs of equations Ax² + By² + Cz² + Dxy + Exz + Fyz + Gx + Hy + Jz + K = 0; when a quadric surface intersects a coordinate plane, the trace is a conic section.

concepts.name: Ellipsoid
concepts.statement: An ellipsoid is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² + z²/c² = 1, all of whose traces are ellipses; a sphere is an ellipsoid with a = b = c.

concepts.name: Elliptic paraboloid
concepts.statement: An elliptic paraboloid is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² = z/c, whose traces include ellipses and parabolas; interchanging the variables gives other orientations.

concepts.name: Hyperboloid of one sheet
concepts.statement: A hyperboloid of one sheet is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² − z²/c² = 1, whose traces include ellipses and hyperbolas; it can be constructed of straight lines.

concepts.name: Hyperboloid of two sheets
concepts.statement: A hyperboloid of two sheets is a surface z²/c² − x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, whose traces include ellipses and hyperbolas.

concepts.name: Elliptic cone
concepts.statement: An elliptic cone is a surface x²/a² + y²/b² − z²/c² = 0, whose traces include ellipses and intersecting lines.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic paraboloid
concepts.statement: A hyperbolic paraboloid is a saddle-shaped surface z/c = x²/a² − y²/b², whose traces include hyperbolas and parabolas.

concepts.name: Sketching a surface from its traces
concepts.statement: To sketch a quadric surface, sketch its traces in the coordinate planes (and in parallel planes where a trace is a single point), which give the framework of the surface.

concepts.name: Identifying quadric surfaces
concepts.statement: To identify the surface of a second-degree equation, look at the signs and powers of x, y and z, completing the square where a variable appears to the first power as well, and match the standard form.

concepts.name: Cylindrical coordinate system
concepts.statement: In the cylindrical coordinate system a point in space is represented by the ordered triple (r, θ, z), where (r, θ) are the polar coordinates of its projection in the xy-plane and z is the usual z-coordinate.

concepts.name: Conversion between cylindrical and rectangular coordinates
concepts.statement: Rectangular and cylindrical coordinates of a point are related by x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, z = z, and r² = x² + y², tan θ = y/x, z = z, θ chosen by the quadrant of (x, y).

concepts.name: Spherical coordinate system
concepts.statement: In the spherical coordinate system a point P in space is represented by (ρ, θ, φ), where ρ is the distance between P and the origin (ρ ≠ 0), θ is the angle of cylindrical coordinates, and φ is the angle between the positive z-axis and the segment OP, 0 ≤ φ ≤ π.

concepts.name: Conversion among spherical, cylindrical and rectangular coordinates
concepts.statement: Spherical and rectangular coordinates are related by x = ρ sin φ cos θ, y = ρ sin φ sin θ, z = ρ cos φ, and ρ² = x² + y² + z², tan θ = y/x, φ = arccos(z/√(x² + y² + z²)); spherical and cylindrical by r = ρ sin φ, θ = θ, z = ρ cos φ, and ρ = √(r² + z²), φ = arccos(z/√(r² + z²)).

concepts.name: Surfaces of constant coordinate
concepts.statement: Holding one coordinate constant gives a surface: in rectangular coordinates x = c, y = c, z = c are planes; in cylindrical coordinates r = c is a vertical circular cylinder, θ = c a half-plane from the z-axis, z = c a plane; in spherical coordinates ρ = c is a sphere, θ = c a half-plane and φ = c a half-cone.

concepts.name: Latitude and longitude
concepts.statement: Latitude and longitude locate points on Earth’s surface as spherical coordinates: with the z-axis through the North Pole and the prime meridian in the xz-plane, longitude east is θ, west negative, and φ is 90° minus the latitude north.

concepts.name: Choosing a coordinate system
concepts.statement: Choose the coordinate system by the problem’s symmetry: spherical coordinates for symmetry about a point, cylindrical coordinates for symmetry about an axis, rectangular coordinates where there is neither, and orient the axes to suit the problem.
